title: Bias, measurement and causality
summary: Three concepts you use to judge any study: whether its measures are reliable and valid, what biases may distort it, and whether it can show cause and effect.

keyterms.definition: A systematic distortion in how research is designed, carried out or interpreted, so results do not reflect reality.
When the researcher's expectations or beliefs influence how data are collected or interpreted.
Cues that let participants guess the aim of a study, so they change their behaviour to fit (or defy) it.
Participants answering or behaving in ways that make them look good rather than truthfully.
Interpreting all behaviour through the norms of one culture, or assuming findings from one culture apply to all.
Defining a variable precisely in terms of how it will be measured or manipulated.
The consistency of a measure: it gives the same results when repeated under the same conditions.
Whether a measure or study actually measures or shows what it claims to.
How confident we can be that changes in the DV were caused by the IV and not by confounding variables.
How far findings reflect behaviour in real-life settings.
A relationship in which a change in one variable produces a change in another.
A relationship between two co-variables; it shows they vary together but not that one causes the other.
An uncontrolled variable that varies with the IV and could explain changes in the DV.
Two variables influence each other, e.g. stress may cause poor sleep and poor sleep may increase stress.

questions.prompt: A researcher who expects a drug to improve mood rates participants' mood after the drug. Which bias is most likely?
questions.explanation: The researcher's expectations can shape their ratings. A double-blind design, where the rater does not know who got the drug, reduces this.

questions.prompt: Which design feature best reduces demand characteristics?
options: Telling participants the hypothesis in advance
Using a single-blind procedure so participants do not know their condition
questions.explanation: If participants cannot work out the aim or their condition, they are less able to change their behaviour to fit it.

questions.statement: Social desirability bias is especially likely when participants answer questions about sensitive topics such as drug use.
questions.explanation: People tend to under-report behaviour that is socially disapproved of. Anonymity and confidential questionnaires can reduce this.

questions.statement: Cultural bias only matters in cross-cultural research.
questions.explanation: Any study that generalizes from one cultural sample to all humans risks cultural bias, e.g. relying mainly on Western undergraduates.

questions.text: When participants guess the aim of a study and change their behaviour, this is caused by ___.
questions.explanation: Demand characteristics are cues in the study that reveal its purpose.

questions.text: Using double-blind procedures mainly reduces ___ bias and participant expectancy.
questions.explanation: In a double-blind design neither the researcher collecting data nor the participant knows the condition.

questions.prompt: Match each bias to a way of reducing it.

pairs.right: Deception about the aim, then debriefing

questions.explanation: Each technique targets the source of a specific bias.

questions.prompt: Much psychology research has used Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic samples. Which concept is this criticism mainly about?
questions.explanation: Over-reliance on WEIRD samples is a form of sampling and cultural bias that limits generalization.

questions.prompt: A researcher interviews people and only notes comments that support her hypothesis. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Selectively noticing confirming data is researcher (confirmation) bias; reflexivity and a second coder help reduce it.

questions.prompt: Which bias is a threat mainly to the participant's side of a study?
questions.explanation: Social desirability comes from participants presenting themselves favourably; researcher bias comes from the researcher.

questions.prompt: "Aggression" is measured as the number of times a child hits a doll in 10 minutes. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Operationalizing turns an abstract variable into something measurable.

questions.prompt: A questionnaire gives very different scores when the same people complete it twice a week apart (with no real change). The questionnaire lacks:
questions.explanation: Consistency over time (test–retest reliability) is low, so the measure is unreliable.

questions.statement: A measure can be reliable without being valid.
questions.explanation: A scale that always reads 2 kg too heavy is consistent (reliable) but wrong (not valid).

questions.statement: A laboratory experiment usually has high ecological validity.
questions.explanation: Lab tasks are often artificial, so behaviour may not reflect real life, although control (internal validity) is high.

questions.text: Checking that two observers give similar scores for the same behaviour tests inter-rater ___.
questions.explanation: High agreement between observers shows the coding scheme is applied consistently.

questions.text: If a study's results could be explained by a confounding variable, its ___ validity is low.
questions.explanation: Internal validity is about whether the IV really caused the change in the DV.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: IV really caused the change in DV
Defining how a variable is measured

questions.explanation: These four ideas make up the concept of measurement.

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to improve the internal validity of an experiment?
questions.explanation: Controlling and randomizing extraneous variables rules out alternative explanations.

questions.prompt: Brain scans measure blood flow, not thinking itself. This is mainly a point about:
questions.explanation: fMRI is an indirect measure, so what it shows about cognition depends on interpretation; this is a measurement issue.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for building a reliable observation scheme in order.
items: Have two observers code the same sample
questions.explanation: Clear categories and training come first; agreement is then checked to establish inter-rater reliability.

questions.prompt: A study finds that teenagers who use social media more report lower mood. What can be concluded?
options: Low mood causes social media use
The two variables are related, but the direction of cause is unknown
questions.explanation: Correlational data cannot show causation; the relationship could be bidirectional or due to a third variable.

questions.prompt: Which research method can establish cause and effect most directly?
questions.explanation: Manipulating the IV while controlling other variables and randomly allocating participants allows causal conclusions.

questions.statement: A correlation coefficient of −0.8 shows a strong relationship.
questions.explanation: The size (0.8) shows strength; the sign shows direction. −0.8 is a strong negative correlation.

questions.statement: If two variables correlate strongly, one must cause the other.
questions.explanation: A third variable may cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental.

questions.text: Stress causing poor sleep, and poor sleep increasing stress, is a ___ relationship.
questions.explanation: In a bidirectional relationship each variable influences the other.

questions.text: Ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in summer because of hot weather; hot weather is a ___ variable.
questions.explanation: A third (confounding) variable can create a correlation between two unrelated variables.

questions.prompt: Match each design to what it can show.

pairs.right: Strength and direction of a relationship
In-depth detail on one person or group
Effect of an IV that occurs naturally

questions.explanation: Only designs where the IV is manipulated with control allow strong causal claims.

questions.prompt: Twin studies can show that a behaviour is partly heritable, but genes may not cause it directly. Why?
options: Genes and environment interact and twins often share environments
Twin studies always use small samples
questions.explanation: Shared environments and gene–environment interaction make it hard to separate genetic causation.

questions.prompt: A researcher randomly allocates participants to conditions. What is the main purpose?
options: To make the sample representative of the population
To spread participant variables evenly so they do not confound results
To make the study more ethical
questions.explanation: Random allocation controls participant variables, protecting internal validity and causal claims.

questions.prompt: Order these from weakest to strongest evidence for a causal claim.
questions.explanation: More control over the IV and allocation of participants strengthens causal inference.
